one_liner: Header-only C++11 lazy-iterator library; first-party 32-element benchmarks show filter 3.6x and chunks 2.6x faster than std::views.
what_it_does: cpp-lazy provides lazy adaptors under the lz:: namespace: map, filter, zip, chunks, chunk_if, split, flatten, take, take_every, cartesian_product, pairwise, repeat and many that std::ranges lacks (except, exclude, intersection, join_where, unique, duplicates, zip_longest, regex_split, random, interleave). They compose with function calls or the | operator and are materialised with lz::to<Container>(). The result is an iterable you can use in range-for and, when it is not sentinelled, in STL algorithms, from C++11 onward. It is a separate API, not a std::ranges implementation, so code written against std::views must be rewritten.
how_it_is_fast: There is no exotic algorithm: the adaptors are thin iterator wrappers that keep as little state as possible. Forward iterables return an lz::default_sentinel_t instead of storing a second end iterator. lz::filter advances by calling the classic std::find_if whenever its iterator and sentinel types match (Lz/detail/algorithm/find_if.hpp), so the scan is the standard library's own find loop. For random-access inputs lz::chunks stores only the chunk start and computes each chunk's end with one min(chunk_size, end - begin) on dereference. The measured gains are code-generation differences against libstdc++'s view iterators on tiny inputs, not a new technique.
when_to_use: C++11/14/17 codebases that want composable lazy map/filter/zip/chunk/split/flatten pipelines without moving to C++20 or pulling in range-v3.

Hot loops that filter or cut contiguous containers into fixed-size chunks: the first-party chart shows these with the largest per-element gaps (3.6x filter, 2.6x chunks vs libstdc++ std::views at gcc 13.3).
You need adaptors std::views does not have (zip_longest, except, intersection, join_where, unique, duplicates, regex_split, random, interleave).
Splitting random-access strings into string_view pieces (lz::sv_chunk_if) without lazy_split's inner-range types.
when_not_to_use: C++20/23 code that mostly uses transform, take, zip, repeat, slide or cartesian_product: the same benchmark shows lz within about 1-4% of std::views there, so there is nothing to gain.
Strided iteration: std::views::stride beat lz::take_every by about 1.7x in the project's own chart.
You rely on std::ranges concepts, projections or views composing with std::ranges algorithms: lz is a separate API, and sentinelled lz iterables need lz::common before classic STL algorithms.

Lifetime-sensitive code: lz iterables keep a reference to any input that does not derive from lz::lazy_view (std::vector, std::array, std::string, user ranges), so they dangle if the input dies first unless wrapped with lz::copied / lz::as_copied.
You need a heavily used, multi-maintainer library: 365 stars, and v9.0.0 broke the API (PascalCase to snake_case, iterators switched to sentinels).

integration.dependencies: none required; {fmt} is optional for printing (the CMake build fetches fmt 12.1.0 unless CPP_LAZY_USE_STANDALONE is set; without CMake define LZ_STANDALONE)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (range-for over sentinelled iterables needs C++17; optional module build needs C++20); CMake 3.14 for the CMake package
integration.platforms: any; README and CI cover GCC, Clang, MSVC and Apple Clang

gotchas: lz::chunk_if drops the delimiter element: tests/chunk_if.cpp expects {1},{3},{5} for an is-even split of {1..5}, while the header's own doc comment shows {1,2},{3,4},{5}. It is not equivalent to std::views::chunk_by, which keeps every element.

Benchmark harness flaws beyond those the verifier found: in the chunk_if row lz emits 31 elements (delimiter 16 dropped) while std::views::chunk_by emits 32, yet both are divided by 32. The split rows compare against std::views::lazy_split, not the C++20 std::views::split meant for contiguous strings. The README says view creation is excluded, but every benchmark builds the view inside the timed loop. No CPU model is given and bench/CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or optimization flags.

Since v9.0.0 many iterables return lz::default_sentinel_t instead of a matching end iterator. Iterate them with range-for on C++17+ or lz::for_each on C++11/14, and call lz::common as late as possible in a chain before handing them to code that needs begin/end of the same type.
CPP_LAZY_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS is on by default in CMake Debug builds and, with GCC/Clang at C++23, links stdc++_libbacktrace. Set it OFF if Debug builds must not carry that dependency.
verified_claims_summary: The project's Google Benchmark 1.9.1 suite builds each adaptor over a 32-element std::array (or 32-char string), walks it once per iteration and reports time per element, with gcc 13.3.0, libstdc++ and C++23. lz::filter took 0.23 vs 0.81 ns per element for std::views::filter (3.6x, predicate matches only the first element), lz::chunks 0.24 vs 0.64 ns for views::chunk (2.6x), split on a char 1.4x over views::lazy_split, and chunk_if and flatten about 1.1x. Most other adaptors were at parity and views::stride was 1.7x faster than lz::take_every; no CPU model or optimization flags are published.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-06, latest release v9.0.1), MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor. The speed claims are first-party microbenchmarks on 32 elements, so it is best treated as a C++11-compatible ranges substitute rather than a proven speedup.
